summary: Sets the IANA rules for allocating new values in the Address Resolution Protocol name spaces, and reserves some numbers for experiments. The changes also affect other protocols that use values from those ARP registries.

eli5.summary: ARP has lists of numbers with special meanings, and someone must decide who gets new ones. This note sets the rules for handing them out and saves a few numbers for people to try out ideas.

questions: how does iana allocate arp numbers
why do arp and dhcp share registries
subtitle: Rules for how IANA hands out new numbers in the Address Resolution Protocol and related protocols

tldr.problem: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) uses several fields with numbered values, but before 2009 there were no clear rules for how IANA should allocate new values to those fields.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies IANA review procedures for each ARP field: some require expert review, others require IETF consensus, and certain values are reserved for experimentation.
tldr.outcome: IANA now has clear, consistent procedures for assigning new values in ARP and in related protocols that share the same registries, such as DHCP, DHCPv6, and several specialized address resolution protocols.

facts.label: Affected protocols
facts.value: ARP, DHCP, DHCPv6, BOOTP, and 6 specialized address resolution protocols

today: RFC 5494 is a Proposed Standard that established the IANA allocation rules for ARP and remains in effect. The procedures it specifies continue to govern how IANA assigns new values in the ARP registries.

sections.title: Overview of ARP and Its Number Spaces
sections.content:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used to discover the hardware address (like a MAC address) associated with an IP address. ARP messages contain several fields that use numbered values, and these numbers come from registries maintained by IANA.

Before this RFC, ARP did not have clear allocation guidelines. This created confusion when new values were requested. The problem was made worse because other important protocols also use the same number registries: DHCP, DHCPv6, BOOTP, and several specialized address resolution protocols for things like ATM, Fibre Channel, and MAPOS.

This RFC establishes clear allocation procedures for ARP's main fields and explains how those procedures affect the related protocols.
sections.eli5: ARP uses lists of numbers, and other protocols use the same lists. Before this, nobody knew how to hand out new numbers fairly, so this document sets the rules.

sections.title: ARP's Number Fields
sections.content:
ARP has three main fields that contain numbered values:

ar$hrd (Hardware address type): A 16-bit field identifying the hardware interface type, such as Ethernet (1), ARCNET (7), or token ring (6). This field is used in several other protocols, including BOOTP and DHCP.

ar$pro (Protocol address type): A 16-bit field that shares values with the Ethertype space (a separate registry for protocol identification numbers).

ar$op (Opcode): A 16-bit field identifying the ARP operation, such as REQUEST (1) or REPLY (2).

Each field has different allocation rules depending on how widely it is used and the need for new values.
sections.eli5: ARP messages have three fields that contain numbers. Each field is a list that IANA keeps.

sections.title: Allocation Rules for Each Field
sections.content:
For ar$hrd (hardware types): Values below 256 or requests for multiple new values require Expert Review. An expert must verify that a need exists and that existing values do not suffice. The expert should assign values above 255 to hardware types that do not need to fit in the 8-bit field of BOOTP/DHCPv4 (since some implementations of those protocols only use 8 bits). For individual new values above 255, First Come First Served allocation is used, and these always get 2-octet values. The expert should assign 1-octet values to types that need to work with BOOTP/DHCPv4.

For ar$pro (protocol types): These numbers are administered through the Ethertype registry (RFC 5342), so ARP allocation rules point to that registry.

For ar$op (opcodes): New values require IETF Review or IESG Approval, the highest level of scrutiny, because opcodes are less frequently requested and changing them is a significant decision.
sections.eli5: Different fields have different approval levels. Some need expert sign-off, some need IETF approval, and some can be handed out on a first-come basis.

sections.title: Reserved Numbers for Experiments
sections.content:
This RFC reserves certain values for experimental and testing purposes. Researchers and implementers can use these values to test new protocol extensions without using permanently allocated values:

For ar$hrd: Two experimental hardware type values are reserved: HW_EXP1 (36) and HW_EXP2 (256). These were chosen deliberately to test both small values (below 256) and large values (above 255), ensuring that implementations handle the full range correctly.

For ar$op: Two experimental opcode values are reserved: OP_EXP1 (24) and OP_EXP2 (25).

Additionally, the values 0 and 65535 are marked as reserved in both ar$hrd and ar$op, meaning they cannot be allocated to any protocol.
sections.eli5: The document saves a few special numbers that people can use to test new ideas without asking permission.

sections.title: How This Affects Other Protocols
sections.content:
Because BOOTP and DHCP use the same hardware address type field as ARP, and DHCPv6 uses a similar field, allocation decisions for ARP's ar$hrd registry affect all of these protocols. If a new hardware type is allocated with a value above 255, it cannot be used in BOOTP or DHCPv4, which only support 8 bits.

Other specialized address resolution protocols also share these registries: they include ATM ARP, HARP (High-Performance Parallel Interface ARP), Fibre Channel ARP, and MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over Synchronous Optical Network) ARP. All of these protocols are therefore affected by the allocation guidelines.

This document ensures that allocation decisions take all of these protocols into account, preventing conflicts and ensuring consistent management.
sections.eli5: When one protocol's number list is shared by many other protocols, the rules have to make sure nothing breaks in any of them.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The allocation rules themselves do not change the security properties of ARP or the affected protocols. However, the RFC warns about experimental values: when someone uses the reserved experimental numbers (HW_EXP1, HW_EXP2, OP_EXP1, OP_EXP2), they must be careful not to deploy experimental code across networks they do not control.

Experimental code points, if deployed carelessly, could cause harmful side effects or unexpected protocol behavior in production networks. The RFC points to RFC 3692 for guidance on the careful use of experimental values.
sections.eli5: New experimental numbers are allowed for testing, but people need to be careful not to break real networks while testing.

sections.title: Why These Rules Matter
sections.content:
Before this RFC, IANA received requests for new ARP values but had no clear procedure. This RFC provides consistency and ensures that allocation decisions are made with full knowledge of the protocols affected. The use of expert review for hardware types ensures that implementations do not pile up with values they cannot use, while IETF review for opcodes ensures that core ARP behavior changes are made deliberately.

By reserving experimental values, the RFC allows the research community to test protocol ideas without consuming allocated values, supporting innovation while maintaining registry discipline.
sections.eli5: Having clear rules means IANA can say yes or no to requests without guessing, and everyone knows what the rules are.
